Rail, roads & fibre · Ghana

Find new digging and building along your railway, road and fibre corridors

Buried cables and railway reserves are easy to dig into and hard to watch, and road corridors fill up as towns grow along them. AfriScan compares dated imagery along your route and flags new excavations, pits, cleared ground and structures inside your wayleave or reserve, so your teams know where to look first. Satellites cannot see a cut cable, theft or people; they show where the ground has changed. A person reviews the results before they reach you.

Send your route See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Long, narrow, and easy to dig into

A railway reserve, a road corridor and a buried cable route have the same weakness: they are long and narrow, and what happens on them is seen only when somebody passes by.

“Someone has been digging along our cable route.”

Road works, building foundations, borrow pits and, in mining districts, galamsey pits can open up along a buried cable. Each shows at the surface as fresh digging, spoil and cleared ground, and each is easier to deal with when it is found early.

“Structures have gone up in the railway reserve.”

Where a line has been quiet for years, sheds, stalls, walls and houses can appear inside the reserve. Before rehabilitation or new services, the operator needs a dated picture of what stands there.

“The widening needs its land counted.”

A road widening or a new alignment starts with how many structures stand within the land it will take, and how that number is changing as towns grow along the road.

“We have to show progress on site.”

Contractors, lenders and supervising engineers need dated evidence of clearing, earthworks and construction between site visits.

Fibre and cable wayleaves

New digging along buried routes, flagged between surveys

A buried fibre route leaves little to see from above, but the ground around it does. We follow the route you send and a band either side of it, and flag fresh excavations, trenches, pits and spoil heaps, cleared ground, new tracks and new structures between dated surveys. A reviewer confirms each flag, and your field teams receive a ranked list of stretches where the ground has changed, with before-and-after views of each.

In gold-mining districts, the same method shows galamsey pits and washing sites opening near the route, as land and water change. Along roads, it shows where other works are digging close to your cable.

Laying a new route is itself regulated: “Cable or Fibre Optic Cable Laying” is one of the undertakings that need an environmental permit under the Environmental Assessment Regulations 2025 (L.I. 2504). A dated baseline along the planned route supports that application, and the first survey after laying becomes the reference for later change.

What satellites can and cannot show

  • Fresh digging, trenches, pits and spoil at the surface
  • Cleared ground, new tracks and new structures
  • Change between two dated surveys

They cannot see a cable, a cut, theft or people. A flag is a reason to check the stretch, not proof of damage.

Railway reserves

What stands inside the reserve, and what crosses it

Railways in Ghana are governed by the Railways Act 2008 (Act 779), under which the Ghana Railway Development Authority works. We list the structures the review confirms inside the reserve width you give us, with their distance to the track centreline or the reserve boundary, their chainage and coordinates, and rate each 500 m segment by the number of structures near the track.

Between surveys, we flag new and removed structures, cleared ground, and new tracks, roads and trenches that cross the reserve. The Act provides for licences for a road or utility line across a railway line, so a list of new crossings, with the date each first appears, helps the railway authority check them.

Before a line is rehabilitated, extended or reopened, a dated register of the reserve is the baseline for engagement and compensation planning, and later surveys record construction progress against it.

What you receive

  • A structure register inside the reserve and in wider bands
  • New crossings of the reserve, with first-seen dates
  • A 500 m segment rating along the line
  • A dated baseline before rehabilitation or extension
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Road corridors

Count the structures before the land take

For a road widening, a new bypass or a new alignment, we count the structures within the distances you set from each option, show how built-up land near each one has grown over recent years, and flag stretches that cross steep, erosion-prone, low-lying or river-crossing ground. Once the alignment is fixed, a dated register of the land it takes becomes the baseline for acquisition and compensation, and re-surveys show what appeared after that date.

Road construction and railway construction both need an environmental permit under L.I. 2504, whose baseline includes a location map of communities, water bodies, forest reserves and sacred groves. We supply those layers to the consultants who prepare the report.

Construction and earthworks

Dated evidence of progress between site visits

Clearing and earthworks

Cleared ground, cuttings and embankments mapped between dated satellite scenes along the whole alignment, stretch by stretch.

Drone detail

Orthophotos and elevation models from drone surveys, compared visit by visit to show where ground was cut or filled, subject to the GCAA authorisations and security clearances each job requires.

Volumes and equipment

Stockpile, spoil and borrow-pit volumes from drone elevation models, and heavy equipment visible on site recorded on each survey date.

Terrain and water

Where the route is exposed to slopes and floods

Steep, erosion-prone and drainage-crossing stretches are highlighted from elevation data, and structures and segments in historically flooded or low-lying ground are flagged, so maintenance and planning teams can see which parts of the route need attention first. After a flood, a map of the flooded area and a reviewer’s before-and-after check of structures along the route show what changed.

How it works

From route file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route and the reserve or wayleave width, and tell us what the record is for: routine checks, a rehabilitation, a new alignment or construction progress.

  2. Screen

    Dated satellite scenes and open building datasets give the first register along the whole route, with no one on site.

  3. Review

    A person confirms each flag and structure, adds what the models missed and lists what the imagery cannot settle.

  4. Repeat

    Re-surveys on the schedule you set, with a change notice after each one, and drone detail where the approvals allow.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map fresh digging, pits, trenches, cleared ground and structures visible from the air
  • Measure each structure to the track, road or cable route
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Compare alignments before a route is fixed

What we don’t do

  • See buried cables, cuts, theft or people
  • Set, survey or verify reserve and wayleave boundaries
  • Decide whether a structure or crossing is authorised
  • Replace patrols, line inspections or field checks

Frequently asked questions

Can you detect a cut cable or damage to the duct?

No. Imagery cannot see a buried cable, a duct or a break in it. We map what is visible at the surface along the route, such as fresh digging, trenches, pits, spoil, cleared ground and new structures, and flag it between surveys so your field teams know which stretches to check.

Which width do you measure along a railway?

The reserve boundary or width you give us, from your own records or the railway authority’s. Each structure carries its exact distance to the track centreline or to the reserve boundary, so the register can be read against any width. We do not set or verify reserve boundaries.

Can you show new crossings of the railway?

Yes, where they are visible: new tracks, roads, paths and trenches across the reserve are flagged between surveys. The Railways Act 2008 (Act 779) provides for licences for a road or utility line across a railway line; whether a particular crossing has one is for the railway authority to check, not for the imagery.

How often can a route be re-surveyed?

On a schedule agreed with you, with a notice after each survey saying what changed and where. Satellites capture images on particular dates, so this is a scheduled record of change, never a constant watch on the route.

Can you help with a new road, railway or cable route?

Yes. We compare alignments side by side by the number of structures within set distances of each one, show where settlement is growing, and flag steep, flood-prone and river-crossing stretches. Road construction, railway construction and cable or fibre-optic cable laying are all undertakings that need an environmental permit under L.I. 2504, and the same layers feed that baseline.

Can you record construction progress?

Yes. Dated satellite scenes show cleared ground and earthworks between dates, and drone orthophotos and elevation models, flown subject to the GCAA authorisations and security clearances each job requires, show cut and fill between visits in detail. Heavy equipment visible on site can be recorded on each survey date.

Send your route

Send the railway, road or cable route (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile or GeoPackage), the reserve or wayleave width, the regions and districts it crosses and the dates the record should cover. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
